# Liquid lace: Regular pattern formation by under-extrusion

Lauren Dreier ,1 Tom Marzin,1 Romain David ,1 Stephane Pienaar,1

Aman Eujayl ,1,2 Raphael Vogeley,1 Yuchen Xi,1 and P.-T. Brun 1

1Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, USA 2Department of Mechanical Engineering, Rice University, Houston, Texas 77005, USA

(Received 10 June 2024; published 22 November 2024)

This paper is associated with a video winner of the 2023 American Physical Society’s Division of Fluid Dynamics (DFD) Milton van Dyke Award for work presented at the DFD Gallery of Fluid Motion. The original video is available online at the Gallery of Fluid Motion, https://doi.org/10.1103/APS.DFD.2023.GFM.V0087.

DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevFluids.9.110512

Fused ﬁlament fabrication (FFF) is a common technique in additive manufacturing. In this methodology, thermoplastic ﬁlament is melted and extruded through a nozzle, depositing a highly viscous thread that rapidly cools—a feature essential for printing in sequential, vertical layers that become three-dimensional objects [1]. Here, we focus on the emergence of periodic patterns when molten ﬁlament material is extruded too slowly in this process. Under-extrusion is often considered

The videos are recorded from the nozzle frame-of-reference, with the substrate moving left to right. [(a)–(f)] Flow rates are held constant while the gap between the nozzle and substrate (illustrated in blue) is sequentially increased until the ﬁlament no longer makes contact. [(g), (h)] High-speed thermal video frames (Infratec ImageIR) for a solid extrusion [(g), e = 1] and under-extrusion [(h), e = 0.4]. See https://doi.org/10.1103/APS.DFD.2023.GFM.V0087.

a defect in FFF printing, typically caused by nozzle clogs, ﬁlament jams, and other issues that prevent adequate ﬁlament ﬂow through the nozzle [2]. However, intentionally under-extruding recasts the instability as a robust manufacturing technique [3,4] for efﬁciently fabricating porous materials without formwork, advanced tooling, or complicated machine control, e.g., for the assembly of textiles [5]. In Fig. 1, we present images showcasing the onset of pattern formation. By reducing the ﬂow rate of molten ﬁlament below a critical value, the extrudate transitions from a solid, adhered thread (a) to a pattern consisting of an adhered region followed by a narrow, unadhered thread (b). Reducing the ﬂow rate further results in a regular pattern (c). The images also show that the pattern is selfstabilizing, where geometric features from the previous row contribute to the stability around a natural wavelength. In Fig. 2, we present high-speed video frames of the instability. In (a)–(f), the pattern forms on a ﬂat substrate positioned at increasing distances from the nozzle, noting the evolution of wavelength and amplitude as the polymer touches, sticks, and stretches. In closing, we note that this pattern complements the rich library of thread-mediated instabilities, including the classic Rayleigh-Plateau instability [6], the breakup of successively printed jets [7,8],

In the case of FFF, we anticipate that the details of pattern formation hinge on a subtle interplay between hydrodynamics, rheology, and cooling [11], as seen in the thermal images in Figs. 2(g) and 2(h).
